mn105:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
mn105:2.1: Now on that occasion final knowledge had been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence:
mn105:2.2: “We understand: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’”
mn105:2.4: “It seems that final knowledge has been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence:
mn105:2.5: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”’”
mn105:3.1: Then Sunakkhatta the Licchavi went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
mn105:4.2: ‘It seems that final knowledge has been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence—
mn105:4.3: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”—so we understand.’
mn105:4.4: Now, venerable sir, do those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge in the Blessed One’s presence:
mn105:4.5: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”’—do they, venerable sir, declare final knowledge rightly, or are there some bhikkhus here who declare final knowledge through overestimation?”
mn105:5.1: “Sunakkhatta, of those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge in my presence:
mn105:5.2: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”’—
mn105:5.3: there are some bhikkhus here who declared final knowledge rightly, but there are also some bhikkhus here who declared final knowledge through overestimation.
mn105:5.4: Now, Sunakkhatta, as to those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge rightly, it is so with them just as they say;
mn105:5.5: but as to those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge through overestimation, in that case, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata:
mn105:5.7: So it is here, Sunakkhatta, that it occurs to the Tathāgata:
mn105:5.9: And yet, here, certain misguided men, having elaborately formulated a question, approach the Tathāgata and ask it.
mn105:5.10: In such a case, Sunakkhatta, even though it had occurred to the Tathāgata:
mn105:5.11: ‘I shall teach them the Dhamma’—there comes to be a change in that intention.”
mn105:6.1: “This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One,
mn105:6.2: for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
mn105:6.3: “Well then, Sunakkhatta, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”
mn105:6.4: “Yes, venerable sir,” Sunakkhatta the Licchavi replied to the Blessed One.
mn105:7.1: “There are, Sunakkhatta, these five cords of sensual desire.
mn105:7.3: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust,
mn105:7.7: tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—
mn105:7.8: these, Sunakkhatta, are the five cords of sensual desire.
mn105:8.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on worldly material things.
mn105:8.2: For a person intent on worldly material things, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:8.3: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:9.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man had long been away from his own village or town.
mn105:9.2: He might see another man who had recently left that village or town.
mn105:9.3: He would ask that man about the safety, plenty, and freedom from sickness of that village or town;
mn105:9.4: and that man would tell him about the safety, plenty, and freedom from sickness of that village or town.
mn105:9.6: would that man listen to that man, give ear, apply his mind to understanding it, associate with that man, and find satisfaction through him?”
mn105:9.8: “So too, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that some individual person here might be intent on worldly material things.
mn105:9.9: For a person intent on worldly material things, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:9.10: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:9.12: ‘This individual person intent on worldly material things is not freed from the fetter of the imperturbable.’
mn105:10.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the imperturbable.[^2]
mn105:10.2: For a person intent on the imperturbable, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:10.3: but when talk connected with worldly material things is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:11.1: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a yellow leaf, fallen from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again;
mn105:11.2: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the imperturbable, the fetter of worldly material things has fallen away.
mn105:11.4: ‘This individual person intent on the imperturbable is freed from the fetter of worldly material things.’
mn105:12.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the base of nothingness.
mn105:12.2: For a person intent on the base of nothingness, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:12.3: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:13.1: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a large rock, split in two, cannot be joined together again;
mn105:13.2: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the base of nothingness, the fetter of the imperturbable is broken.
mn105:13.4: ‘This individual person intent on the base of nothingness is freed from the fetter of the imperturbable.’
mn105:14.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn105:14.2: For a person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:14.3: but when talk connected with the base of nothingness is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:15.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man had eaten delicious food and then vomited it up.
mn105:15.3: would that man have any desire to eat that food again?”
mn105:15.6: “Because, venerable sir, that food is now reckoned as disgusting.”
mn105:15.7: “So too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the fetter of the base of nothingness has been vomited up.
mn105:15.9: ‘This individual person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is freed from the fetter of the base of nothingness.’
mn105:16.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be rightly intent on Nibbāna.
mn105:16.2: For a person rightly intent on Nibbāna, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;
mn105:16.3: but when talk connected with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.
mn105:17.1: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of growing again;
mn105:17.2: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person rightly intent on Nibbāna, the fetter of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has been cut off, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no more subject to future arising.
mn105:17.4: ‘This individual person rightly intent on Nibbāna is freed from the fetter of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’
mn105:18.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:
mn105:18.2: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic;[^3] the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.
mn105:18.3: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’
mn105:18.4: He might conceive this though it is not really so.
mn105:18.5: He would pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.
mn105:18.6: As he pursues an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would invade his mind.
mn105:18.7: With his mind invaded by lust, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.
mn105:19.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.
mn105:19.2: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring a surgeon to treat him.
mn105:19.3: The surgeon would cut round the opening of the wound with a knife.
mn105:19.4: Having cut round the opening of the wound with a knife, he would probe for the arrow with a probe.
mn105:19.5: Having probed for the arrow with a probe, he would pull out the arrow, and remove the poison, but with some trace remaining.[^4]
mn105:19.6: Knowing that some trace remained, he would say:
mn105:19.7: ‘Good man, your arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, but with some trace remaining.
mn105:19.8: It is not enough to endanger you.
mn105:19.9: Eat only suitable food; do not let unsuitable food make your wound discharge.
mn105:19.10: Wash the wound from time to time, and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, lest, from your not washing the wound and not anointing the opening of the wound from time to time, stale blood should seal up the opening of the wound.
mn105:19.11: And do not walk about in the wind and sun, lest, as you walk about in the wind and sun, dust and grit should infect the opening of the wound.
mn105:19.12: You must live guarding the wound, good man, until it heals.’
mn105:20.2: ‘My arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with some trace remaining.
mn105:20.3: It is not enough to endanger me.’
mn105:20.4: And he would eat unsuitable food, and from his eating unsuitable food his wound would discharge.
mn105:20.5: And he would not wash the wound from time to time, nor anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, and from his not doing so, stale blood would seal up the opening of the wound.
mn105:20.6: And he would walk about in the wind and sun, and from his doing so, dust and grit would infect the opening of the wound.
mn105:20.7: And he would not live guarding the wound, nor let it heal.
mn105:20.8: Then, both through this unsuitable conduct and through the impure poison that had been removed but with some trace remaining, the wound would swell up from these two causes.
mn105:20.9: With the wound swollen up in this way, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.

mn105:21.2: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic; the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.
mn105:21.3: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’
mn105:21.4: He might conceive this though it is not really so.
mn105:21.5: He would pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.
mn105:21.6: As he pursues an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would invade his mind.
mn105:21.7: With his mind invaded by lust, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.
mn105:22.1: For, Sunakkhatta, in the Discipline of the Noble Ones, this is death: when one abandons the training and reverts to the lower life;
mn105:22.2: and this, Sunakkhatta, is suffering close to death: when one commits a certain defiled offence.
mn105:23.1: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:
mn105:23.2: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic; the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.
mn105:23.3: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’
mn105:23.4: Being one who is truly rightly intent on Nibbāna, he would not pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would not pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would not pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would not pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would not pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would not pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.
mn105:23.5: As he does not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would not invade his mind.
mn105:23.6: With his mind not invaded by lust, he would meet neither death nor suffering close to death.
mn105:24.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn105:24.5: Having probed for the arrow with a probe, he would pull out the arrow, and remove the poison, with no trace remaining.
mn105:24.6: Knowing that no trace remained, he would say:
mn105:24.7: ‘Good man, your arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with no trace remaining.

mn105:24.11: And do not walk about in the wind and sun, lest, as you walk about in the wind and sun, dust and grit should infect the opening of the wound.
mn105:24.12: You must live guarding the wound, good man, until it heals.’
mn105:25.2: ‘My arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with no trace remaining.
mn105:25.3: It is not enough to endanger me.’
mn105:25.4: And he would eat only suitable food, and from his eating suitable food his wound would not discharge.
mn105:25.5: And he would wash the wound from time to time, and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, and from his doing so, stale blood would not seal up the opening of the wound.

mn105:25.7: And he would live guarding the wound, and let it heal.

mn105:25.9: With the wound healed and covered over with skin, he would meet neither death nor suffering close to death.

mn105:27.1: This simile, Sunakkhatta, has been made by me to convey a meaning.
mn105:27.3: ‘wound’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for the six internal bases;
mn105:27.4: ‘poison’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for ignorance;
mn105:27.5: ‘dart’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for craving;
mn105:27.6: ‘probe’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for mindfulness;
mn105:27.7: ‘knife’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for noble wisdom;
mn105:27.8: ‘surgeon’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.
mn105:28.1: Truly, Sunakkhatta, a bhikkhu who practises restraint in the six bases of contact,
mn105:28.2: and who, knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’[^5] is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.
mn105:29.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, there were a bronze cup of a drink, endowed with colour, endowed with smell, endowed with taste;
mn105:29.2: but it was mixed with poison.
mn105:29.3: Then a man came along who wanted to live, did not want to die, wanted happiness, and recoiled from suffering.
mn105:29.5: would that man drink from that cup of drink, knowing:
mn105:29.6: ‘Having drunk this, I will meet death, or suffering close to death’?”
mn105:29.8: “So too, Sunakkhatta, when a bhikkhu, practising restraint in the six bases of contact,
mn105:29.9: and knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’ is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.
mn105:30.1: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, there were a fierce, venomous snake.
mn105:30.2: Then a man came along who wanted to live, did not want to die, wanted happiness, and recoiled from suffering.
mn105:30.4: would that man give his hand or his thumb to that fierce, venomous snake, knowing:
mn105:30.5: ‘Bitten by this, I will meet death, or suffering close to death’?”
mn105:30.7: “So too, Sunakkhatta, when a bhikkhu, practising restraint in the six bases of contact,
mn105:30.8: and knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’ is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—
mn105:30.9: it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.”
mn105:30.10: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn105:30.11: Sunakkhatta the Licchavi was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
